metadata.title: Have You Asked the Chatbot About Your Brand Lately? It's the new first impression, and it takes five minutes to check.
metadata.topic: AI & BRANDS · THE NEW FIRST IMPRESSION
metadata.register: Warm, simple, friendly -- short sentences, no jargon; positive but fair, and clear about which numbers come from companies, per the user's explicit tone request.
metadata.note: Sourced from the user-supplied article 'Have You Asked the Chatbot About Your Brand Lately?' (pasted directly in the build request; 6 references: BrandMentions 'How to check what ChatGPT says about your brand' (2026); CloudNine PR press release on ChatGPT and brand discovery (2026); Sanbi 'Inaccurate AI claims about your brand' (2026); Searchable 'The AI brand misinformation report' (Jul 30 2026); SubscribePR 'ChatGPT says wrong things about your business' (2026); Yext 'Cracking the ChatGPT code' (2026) -- see FACTCHECK.md). User asked for a 'Deep Explainer' at exactly 4:00. The toolkit's actual deep-explainer skill targets 5-10 min and requires ~20-25% of body beats to be pantry/archival stills sourced through a two-gate pipeline. Both conflict with this request: a hard 4:00 target, and the user's own note that no footage exists for this article. Built instead on the ai-explainer chassis (Claude composer cold open -> presenter intro -> body -> handoff -> outro), reusing the all-self-generated Manim/Remotion approach and af_bella/@HumanitariansAI branding used on this user's other reels. The host self-introduction ('Hi, I'm Agrima') lives in its own B00B presenter-intro beat, matching this user's other ai-explainer-chassis builds. HEDGING (per the user's explicit request and the article): every statistic is attributed to its source on its stat card and, where it fits, in narration (the 900 million, Pew and 'more than 25 million links' figures come secondhand through BrandMentions; the 4% to 7% figure comes through Sanbi from a Profound study; the Searchable results were graded by the brands themselves); the two headline error numbers (3 in 4 brands vs 4% to 7% of claims) are explained as answering two different questions; and a closing spoken note plus an on-screen sources card say most sources are companies that sell marketing, PR, or brand-monitoring services, so the statistics are industry-reported, not independent research. The bakery scene is labeled on screen and in narration as an illustration, not a reported case. NO real brand or company logos are used (source names appear only as plain text; 'Maple Street Bakery' is the article's own invented example); every visual is a generated Manim graphic. The user's explicit tone request (warm, simple, friendly; positive but fair) is a deliberate departure from this chassis's default Teardown register -- disclosed here.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- ask shown answered; no self-intro here (see B00B)
beats.narration_text: I asked Claude to help me picture a simple moment: what would a chatbot say about a bakery?

props.command:
claude "what would a chatbot say about a
  small bakery on my street?"
props.segment: Have You Asked the Chatbot Lately?
output: they ask a chatbot instead of the map

beats.role_note: presenter intro -- 'Hi, I'm Agrima' + lead-in; doubles as the EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY beat
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. Today: asking the chatbot about your brand. It's the new first impression, and it takes five minutes to check.
beats.visual_intent: presenter card: name, then a short lead-in

beats.role_note: someone hears about a small bakery from a friend, skips the map, asks a chatbot 'What's good at Maple Street Bakery, and when is it open?', decides whether to visit from the answer; labeled an illustration -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Someone hears about a small bakery from a friend. They skip the map and ask a chatbot: what's good at Maple Street Bakery, and when is it open? They decide whether to visit based on what it says. This is an illustration, not a real case. But it's becoming a very ordinary moment.
beats.visual_intent: a cozy bakery storefront beside a phone showing a chat: the question typed, a confident answer appearing; 'illustration -- not a real case' label

beats.role_note: ChatGPT passed 900 million weekly users in Feb 2026; Pew: 49% of U.S. adults have used an AI chatbot, 42% to look up information; UK survey of 2,564 consumers Apr 2026: 78% use AI chat tools, 52% of those say they help find new brands; for many brands the chatbot is a first impression -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: That's the new front door. ChatGPT passed nine hundred million weekly users in February. Pew found that forty-nine percent of U.S. adults have used an AI chatbot. And in one U.K. survey, fifty-two percent of users said these tools help them find brands they would not have discovered otherwise. For many brands, the chatbot is now a first impression.
beats.visual_intent: three stat cards, each with its source: 900 million (weekly users), 49% / 42% (Pew via BrandMentions), 78% / 52% (UK survey, CloudNine PR)

beats.act: BEAT 3 — what it says may not be quite right
beats.role_note: 1,704 brands graded 32,556 facts; about 3 in 4 brands found at least one false fact; small organizations ~50% more often than large firms; pricing, funding, which tools it works with most often wrong -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: But what it says may not be quite right. In one large review, seventeen hundred brands graded thirty-two thousand facts AI tools stated about them. About three in four brands found at least one false fact. Small organizations saw false facts about fifty percent more often than large firms. Pricing, funding, and which tools a product works with were most often wrong.
beats.visual_intent: a 3-in-4 brand graphic (three flagged, one clear), a small-vs-large organizations bar, three chips for most-often-wrong facts; source chip Searchable 2026, brands graded their own facts

beats.role_note: a different study counted claims, not brands: ~4% to 7% wrong; the numbers don't conflict: 'did any mistake show up?' vs 'how many statements were wrong?'; mostly right, mistakes worth catching -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: A different study counted claims, not brands, and found about four to seven percent were wrong. The two numbers do not conflict. One asks: did any mistake show up? The other asks: how many statements were wrong? Chatbots are mostly right, with mistakes worth catching.
beats.visual_intent: two question cards: 'did any mistake show up?' -> 3 in 4 brands vs 'how many statements were wrong?' -> 4% to 7% (a row of dots, illustrative); both sourced

beats.role_note: most errors aren't made up; they trace to real pages (old pricing page, outdated review, old comparison article); in more than half of the brands studied the brand's own pages were among the sources; some chatbots answer from memory that stops at a training date -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Here's the encouraging part. Most errors are not made up. They trace back to real pages. An old pricing page. An outdated review. An old comparison article. In more than half of the brands studied, the brand's own pages were among the sources. Some chatbots also answer from memory that stops at a training date, so a new address or price may be missing.
beats.visual_intent: an old pricing page, an outdated review and an old comparison article feeding arrows into a chatbot answer; a 'more than half' card for the brand's own pages; a training-date memory chip

beats.act: BEAT 4b — what others say about you
beats.role_note: analysis of 25M+ AI-cited links: coverage written by others made up most citations (BrandMentions); ~53% of ChatGPT citations from managed listings like business profiles vs ~40% from brand websites (Yext); profiles and reviews matter as much as your own site -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: AI tools also lean on what others say about you. In an analysis of more than twenty-five million AI-cited links, coverage written by others made up most citations. In another, about fifty-three percent of ChatGPT's citations came from managed listings, like business profiles, and forty percent from brand websites. So profiles and reviews matter as much as your website.
beats.visual_intent: a 25 million+ links card (most citations: coverage written by others) and a 53% vs 40% two-bar card (managed listings vs brand websites); both sourced

beats.role_note: survey of 3,848 people: 95% took at least one extra step before acting on an AI recommendation (Yext); only 4% of UK AI users would buy from an unfamiliar brand right away (CloudNine PR); chatbot opens the door, website and reviews do the rest; if they disagree a visitor may wonder which to believe -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: People do double-check. In a survey of thirty-eight hundred people, ninety-five percent took at least one extra step before acting on an AI recommendation. And only four percent of U.K. AI users would buy from an unfamiliar brand right away. The chatbot opens the door. Your website and reviews do the rest. If they disagree, a visitor may wonder which to believe.
beats.visual_intent: a 95% stat card with three extra-step chips, a 4% stat card with a small meter; footer: the chatbot opens the door; your website and reviews do the rest

beats.role_note: the requested numbered checklist that builds step by step: ask two or three chatbots; ask like a customer; note right, wrong, missing and sources; fix it at the source; check again in a few weeks -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: Here's the five-minute check. One: ask two or three different chatbots, since the same mistake rarely shows up everywhere. Two: ask like a customer would. What is it? What does it cost? Where is it, and when is it open? Is it any good? What are the alternatives? Three: note what's right, wrong, and missing, and any sources named. Four: fix it at the source. Update old pricing pages, hours, and addresses, and make sure your profiles and review sites match each other and your website. Five: check again in a few weeks.
beats.visual_intent: the requested checklist graphic: five numbered rows build one by one with a tick each; step two shows five customer-question chips; step four shows the sources to fix

beats.role_note: not about gaming a chatbot; about making sure accurate, current information is easy to find; for small teams, nonprofits and local organizations, a five-minute check can keep wrong hours or an old address from becoming someone's first impression; a small team looking at an accurate profile -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: This isn't about gaming a chatbot. It's about making sure accurate, current information is easy to find. For small teams, including nonprofits and local organizations, a five-minute check can keep wrong hours or an old address from becoming someone's first impression.
beats.visual_intent: the requested closing scene: a small team looks at an accurate business profile on a screen (hours, address, prices all ticked); closing lines; 'illustration' label

beats.role_note: most sources are companies that sell marketing, PR or brand-monitoring services, so the statistics are industry-reported, not independent research; one study was graded by the brands themselves; six sources listed; the bakery scene is an illustration -- SHOW
beats.narration_text: A note on sources. Most come from companies that sell marketing, PR, or brand-monitoring services, so the statistics are industry-reported, not independent research. And one study was graded by the brands themselves.
beats.visual_intent: a sources card (six sources as plain text, no logos) with an on-screen note: industry-reported, not independent research; one study graded by the brands themselves; the bakery scene is an illustration

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- suggested prompt typed in, viewer-addressed, read aloud and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Ask two or three chatbots about your own brand, or an organization you care about. Note what's right, wrong, and missing.

claude "what would a customer learn about my
  brand from a chatbot? what is right, wrong, missing?"
props.segment: Have You Asked the Chatbot Lately?

beats.role_note: OUTRO LAW -- restate the title, last beat, source citation
beats.narration_text: Have you asked the chatbot lately? It takes five minutes. Full citations are in the description.
